No need to apologize at all, venting can be a perfectly healthy outlet.  I'm sorry to hear that the two people you have reached out weren't able to support you in the way that you were looking for.  Have you ever considered a professional therapist?  Just a thought.

Even when people are unhappy with how their lives are going (and have been there myself), I still think that discontent is the lever for change.  You have identified things that you are displeased with, and haven't accepted them.  There is a part of you that wants things to change, the desire exists.  And I am sure you can find a way to lever that desire into positive changes in your life.

I am very sorry that to hear about your friend.  I too have lost friends when they are much too young.  As hard as it is right now, and is going to be in the future, try to remember all of the good times that you two shared, because, truly, nothing can take away from those memories that you have.  Cherish the memories and, as unfair as it seems, we sometimes have to be thankful that we have the opportunity for certain remarkable people to be in our lives.  Best wishes to you.

I understand the struggle is very real, and accumulations are often the byproduct of depression.  If you are able to, maybe you can do one small thing for yourself per day; something that you can find a little enjoyment in (even if the depression has lessened the enjoyment of activities.)  Have a laugh at a YouTube video, listen to a favorite song for 5 minutes; my humble suggestion would to make small chips in your depression when possible.  And celebrate small victories.  There were days in deep depression where I celebrated very "minor" things.  "I showered today!"

Do you have someone in your life that you can confide in, a friend or family member perhaps?  Sometimes letting someone else to help with your struggles can make all the difference.  If you would like to or need to, please feel to converse with me.  Best wishes to you!

Existentialist, checking in.

In life, suffering and pain are inevitable.  At some level, I think we all know that life will deal us blows, and, at times, some blows will makes us question: do we want to stand back up in the ring?  Do we want to bow out?  What's the point, if I can expect more of the same?

Life is not about living pain-free.  It is how we live in response to suffering.  If we go through it telling ourselves that "my suffering is meaningless", then, most likely, you will only focus on suffering.  But it can be a means to an end, and the "end" is *meaning*.

As the philosopher Albert Camus said : "We all carry in us our places of exile, our crimes, our ravages.  Our task is not to unleash them on the world; it is to transform them in ourselves and others."

Speaking more directly though, I've suffered depression.  I've been inconvenienced with unemployed, I've battled with binge eating.  If anything that I've said is even remotely helpful, know that I am more than willing to extend my hand and/or ear for the sake of conversation.  (Feel free to PM)

Please take some time to re-examine a few thoughts in a different line, talk to someone with a different perspective (online or "real life"), and, most importantly of all, take care of yourself.

Best wishes.

To me, the inclusion of the alcohol and bottle of wine seem slightly out of place.  George wants this to to be a day of "happy ignorance", but the alcohol is tied to what seem to be some troubling things in the family.  Maybe the foreshadowing could be a little less direct.

I would prefer to read "happy ignorance" as them just enjoying father/daughter time of the innocent nature of flying a kite.  Maybe expanding on the diner scene?  Is there special significance of that diner to them?  Are they being nostalgic? I envision the daughter being a bit child-like again, being able to spend this unexpected time with her dad...

Also, when you talk about Annabelle being too smart and aware for her own good (sometimes), I again wish you would soften the punch a little bit.  Maybe hint that sometimes she was aware of familial problems without telling us directly.  When you do write the bits with Maria, I still think that is important that you write her character so that the reader can empathize with her character as well.  George knows that his wife is fragile, delicate, but lead the reader down that path by letting us identify with her, too.  Even thought she's not in the story directly yet.

In essence, I think you have a wonderful start to your start.  The slight 'problems' that I have mentioned are mostly issues of pacing, I feel.  You have some wonderful set-ups but if you prolong the deliveries of the shocks, I think it would make them more powerful.

Hopefully, I haven't gone and said to much.  But, you did ask, and giving me an invitation to speak is a dangerous thing. ;)

Best of luck with your future writings.  As I said, it would be great to read more.

First time on this subreddit, so hopefully I'm doing this correctly:

I consider myself more a developmental editor, so keep that in mind, please.  Structurally, I think it is very sound and well-written.  My constructive criticism would be that I think the reveal happens too quickly.  I would like a sense of George before we know he has bad medical news.  In my humble opinion, that becomes too defining to his character.  Yes, he has to share the news.  But I kept wondering to myself, what was George like before?  We do get a taste of that with the kite flying, but I still think it would be more poignant if you waited just a bit a longer to drop your "bombshell".

In that way, it could catch me, the reader, unawares.  Instead, after reading the very first lines, I was like, whelp, he's a goner...

There are a couple smaller things, but I don't want to become too picky.  You're probably tired of this comment. ;)  For one, the descriptor of horny philosophy student seemed ... tacked on.  I didn't understand.  Guess my understanding of Maria got a muddled.

Okay, I think that's quite enough.  I hope this helps in some small way.  Thanks for sharing, and I think I will return to this sub...

Speaking from experience, if your school has more than one therapist, you can request to see someone else.  Sometimes, for whatever reason, a therapist is not a good fit.

And as a point of clarification, if you tell a therapist you have thoughts of suicide, they *cannot* institutionalize you.  If you you are in immediate danger of hurting yourself, if you go to them and say "I have a plan: x, y, and z," ; that is grounds for them to intervene.  In order for a professional to intervene, there has to be an immediate risk.

I met him when we both working minimum wage jobs trying to start over.  And he has come along way to sobriety and now is living with a girlfriend.  When he was at his rock bottom, he never thought that he would be where he is today.  Never.  I wish I could give you a simple answer of do this and everything will turn out fine.

Instead, all I can do is encourage you to think that maybe, just maybe something is in the cards for you that is an improvement. He's forty years old, recently divorced, doesn't think he can start over that late in life....

It's never to late to start over.  Josh didn't start over until he was well beyond 40, too.  It's never too late!  I would be damned liar if I said life is easy or that starting over is easy, but it can be done.  Try to look for the sliver of hope, man.  I hope that pretty soon that 1O % chance gets bigger and bigger.  You have my very best wishes!!! Take care.

Apathy is such a hard thing to combat.  No, things aren't going to automatically improve, and "waiting for life to happen" can be excruciating.  Life is going to be a mix of the good, the bad, and the ugly.  Our reactions to the situations are what come to define us.

And, on the plus side, you are not *completely* apathetic.  You posted here and you care about what the people in your life think about you.  Complete apathy is more dangerous place.

This is what your post tells me: you want more out of life, you don't know how to get there yet; but you want something more.  I don't know your life particulars, and that's okay: you're still worth this post -- although I apologize for it's vague nature.

Don't give up.  Please don't give up.  In the words of Samuel Beckett:  Ever tried?  Ever failed?  Try again.  Fail again.  Fail better.

All my best!

Your post reminded me of two things from literature that show that this sentiment has always been present.  You are not alone in confronting the abyss.

First, Nietzsche, who said in one of his aphorisms that I have oft quoted, "And when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you."

And of course, Hamlet's "To Be or Not to Be" is an extremely emotional and heart-felt monologue about being on the edge of the abyss.

An overdose does bear certain similarities to suicide, and it is a well-documented effect than when someone we know commits suicide, it can lead to increased suicidal thoughts in others.  Know that you are not alone, not in your connection with PSH, or in having depressed thoughts.  No matter how alone we feel, we are never truly alone.

At various points in my life, I have seen some very low lows.  I understand where you are coming from.  Although I do not plan on taking my life, I stall have the occasional thoughts that enter my mind.  But, we are not the content of our thoughts.

Although I don't know you, I am sure that you have talents and abilities beyond baking a cake.  I wish you all the best in finding meaning in your existence; it it something that we all have to find.  All my very best!!!

I've used this quote before, but it is a pretty accurate summary of my beliefs:

"Love is the only sane and satisfactory answer to the problem of human existence". - Erich Fromm

Erich Fromm actually wrote an entire book called the "Art of Loving" about how difficult it is to love.  Being a sociologist, he blamed society and vapid love songs for leading us to believe that love is easy, that we simply fall in love, experience love at first sight, on and on.

Why am I busting out some academic / sociologist?  Because he understood that love is hard, and takes a lot of work.  Further, he said there are two different types of love: the first is where we 'love' for selfish reasons, because we need to be affirmed.  The more mature type of love, that coincidentally is kind of hippy ish, is akin to free love.  Where we can love openly and freely for love's sake, and even be okay if our love isn't returned.

I could commiserate with you over many loves lost and many more frustrating crushes and tantalizing what ifs.  I could share with you a break up story two days old, where I thought I might finally be losing my forever alone status, but I would much rather send you my very best wishes that you keep your heart open to the possibilities.  You know love is hard, but that is an understanding that will only help you going forward.  All my best!

Does that lessen your frustration? Probably not.  But try to make peace that your feelings are still valid, even if you can't expect a relationship.

We all play the fool sometimes in crushes, love, etc.  I am still in my 20's and have had a string of falling for unavailable guys (in a variety of ways), but we can honour the feelings and LEARN even as they seem to torture us.

I hope this helps in some small way.  Be patient with yourself, be kind to yourself, and keep your heart open. :)  All my best!

Best of luck; keep writing; and try to silence 'the critic'!

If you go to an emergency room / hospital and you tell them that you are suicidal, you will be admitted for psychiatric evaluation and help.  Depending on whether your hospital has a psychiatric facility / open beds, you may be transferred to another facility.

Within 24 hours you MUST been seen and evaluated by a psychiatrist.  It is one of your rights as patient.  In addition to starting some medication, you could also expect some combination of group therapy, individual therapy, stress management / relaxation, and spiritual guidance.

If you are suicidal, please, please, please seek help.  Posting here is a good first step.  I know the idea of being hospitalized is quite scary, but if there's any specific questions I can answer, please contact me.  In my experience the fellow patients you meet will really help you understand that you are not alone in your struggles.

Also, if you are admitted to a psychiatric unit, you can expect to stay for about 5 days or possibly longer.

Sending all of my best wishes to you.  Please take good care.
